Spoiler alert, in case you haven't seen the movie yet but had planned on it. Gonna keep this short.

First off, their execution of representation is subtle and realistic, not hamfisted and gratuitous like most modern productions. Atlantis was (and still is) an ethnostate, but was broken up into different tribes during its fall. Over time, the tribes evolved in differing ways; the nominal Atlantis continuing to be Anglican in appearance, and other tribes evolving into humanoid creatures of the deep. The movie doesn't muddy this arc by gratuitously throwing in Atlanteans of color; instead, it draws its diversity from a faction of African American bandits. But it doesn't make the mistake of overtly denouncing the ethnostate, nor of favoring it. Instead, we discover through the dialogue of the Atlanteans a colored history of violence and triumph, of achievement and disregard, and of a system which is so orderly as to have guaranteed societal success, but at the cost of individual agency. By the end, it is clear that Aquaman's ascension from outsider/half-breed/bastard to kinghood, followed by the untraditional sparing of his brother, is a good thing for Atlantis, and that there will be a series of changes needed to open up the society to be more free and less punishing.

At first, I thought the movie would catch flak for its most prominent people of color being not only "the bad guys," but irredeemable thieves. That changes, though, when the eventual antihero "Black Manta" has to abandon his father to certain death on board a robbery-gone-wrong, in which Aquaman could have saved the father but explicitly chooses not to. This presents the viewer with a moral dilemma, of sympathizing with the sentimental moment of a violent criminal, and seeing their beloved hero in a negative light. Black Manta's quest for revenge is also one of the more forgivable, as his singular target is Aquaman, and he doesn't cause any innocent casualties in his pursuit. Furthermore, Aquaman explicitly expresses that he was wrong to not save Black Manta's father, and that his hatred is justifiable.

Obviously there are a lot of other aspects to representation, but these are the memorable takeaways that made me feel it was the first movie in a while to walk the line subtly and successfully.
